title: Elections and Political Participation
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about how a vote becomes a seat, why the rules of the game change who wins, and the many ways citizens take part in democracy beyond election day.
competenceGoals: discuss the importance of democratic participation and citizens' rights and duties
analyse how electoral systems affect representation and political outcomes

content.content:
## The same votes, a different government

Here is a puzzle. Imagine an election where one party wins forty percent of the national vote, another wins thirty-five, and a third wins twenty-five. Who should govern? You might assume the answer is fixed by the votes -- but it is not. Depending on the rules a country uses to turn votes into seats, that exact same result could produce a single-party government with a comfortable majority, or a coalition of parties forced to share power. The votes did not change. The *system* did.

Elections are the lifeblood of democracy: they let citizens choose leaders and hold them accountable. But the machinery that translates votes into power -- the **electoral system** -- quietly shapes everything from how many parties survive to how closely the government reflects what people actually wanted. And as we will see, voting is only one of many ways to take part.

## How votes become seats: two great families

The electoral system is the set of rules deciding how citizens' votes turn into seats in the legislature, and two families dominate. The first is **first-past-the-post (FPTP)**, used in the UK, the US, Canada and India. The country is carved into single-member districts, and in each one the candidate with the most votes wins -- even with less than half the total. Its strengths are simplicity, a strong link between a representative and a local area, and a tendency to produce clear majorities and stable governments. Its weakness is that results can be wildly disproportionate: in the 2019 UK general election, the Liberal Democrats won about 11.5 percent of the national vote but only 1.7 percent of the seats. Under a proportional system they would have taken roughly 75 seats instead of 11.

The second family is **proportional representation (PR)**, used in Norway, Sweden, the Netherlands and Germany. Here seats are handed out in proportion to each party's share of the vote, so smaller parties can win representation and fewer votes are "wasted." The trade-off is that parliaments may fragment into many parties and require coalition governments, which some find less stable, and the link to a specific local district is weaker. Some countries split the difference: Germany's mixed-member proportional system gives voters two ballots, one for a local candidate and one for a party list. Run our opening puzzle through both: under PR the three parties get roughly 40, 35 and 25 seats and must form a coalition; under FPTP the leading party might sweep to around 55 seats and govern alone on 40 percent support. Neither outcome is simply "right" -- they reflect different values, stability versus representativeness.

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: Under first-past-the-post, how is the winner in each district decided?

options.text: The candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority
The candidate with more than 50 percent always wins
Seats are shared in proportion to the vote
The party leader chooses

questions.solution: In FPTP the candidate with the most votes in a single-member district wins the seat, even if that is less than half of all votes cast.

questions.task: What is a key advantage of proportional representation?

options.text: It always produces single-party majority governments
Seats reflect each party's share of the vote, so fewer votes are wasted
It eliminates the need for elections
It guarantees the largest party governs alone

questions.solution: PR allocates seats in proportion to vote share, allowing smaller parties to win representation and reducing wasted votes.

questions.task: The 2019 UK example, where a party won 11.5 percent of votes but 1.7 percent of seats, illustrates which feature of FPTP?

options.text: Its tendency to produce highly proportional results
That it bans small parties
Its tendency to produce disproportionate results
That it uses ranked-choice voting

questions.solution: It shows how FPTP can be highly disproportionate, leaving smaller parties with far fewer seats than their vote share would suggest.

questions.task: Why does the chapter say neither FPTP nor PR is simply "right"?

options.text: Because both are illegal
Because they always give identical results
Because only experts can use them
Because they reflect different values -- stability versus representativeness

questions.solution: FPTP tends to favour stability and clear majorities, while PR favours representativeness; the choice reflects which democratic value a society prioritises.

content.content:
## Democracy beyond the ballot box

Voting is the most visible act of citizenship, but a healthy democracy runs on far more. **Conventional participation** includes joining a political party and attending its meetings, contacting your elected representatives, running for office yourself, volunteering on a campaign, or donating to a cause. **Unconventional but legal participation** widens the picture further: signing petitions, joining demonstrations and protests, boycotting products for political reasons, joining interest groups or NGOs, using social media to raise awareness, and even **civil disobedience** -- deliberately breaking an unjust law to protest it, as the American Civil Rights Movement famously did.

One useful health check is **voter turnout** -- the share of eligible citizens who actually vote. It varies a lot: around 91 percent in Australia, where voting is compulsory, about 77 percent in Norway, roughly 67 percent in the UK, around 62 percent in the US in the unusually high 2020 election, and only about 45 percent in Switzerland, which holds frequent referendums instead. Turnout is shaped by age (younger voters tend to vote less), education, socioeconomic status, how competitive the election is, how easy registration is, and whether voting is required by law. Low turnout can signal apathy, disillusionment, or real barriers to taking part. The deeper point is that democracy is not just something that happens on election day every few years -- it depends on citizens staying engaged in the long stretches between, through the many channels open to them.

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: Which of these is an example of unconventional but legal participation?

options.text: Joining a peaceful protest or signing a petition
Voting in a general election
Running for office
Donating to a party

questions.solution: Protests, petitions, boycotts and similar actions are unconventional but legal forms of participation, distinct from conventional acts like voting or running for office.

options.text: The number of parties in an election
The share of eligible citizens who actually vote
The number of candidates per district
The age at which people can vote

questions.solution: Turnout is the percentage of eligible citizens who cast a ballot, often used as a rough measure of democratic engagement.

questions.task: Why does Australia have very high voter turnout (around 91 percent)?

options.text: Because it uses first-past-the-post
Because it has no political parties
Because voting is compulsory
Because elections are secret

questions.solution: Australia has compulsory voting, with fines for not voting, which pushes turnout to around 91 percent.

questions.task: What is civil disobedience as described in the chapter?

options.text: Voting against the government
Refusing to pay any taxes ever
Joining a political party
Deliberately breaking an unjust law to protest it

questions.solution: Civil disobedience means deliberately and openly breaking a law considered unjust as a form of protest, as in the US Civil Rights Movement.

content.content:
## In short

Electoral systems quietly shape democracy by deciding how votes become seats. First-past-the-post, used in the UK and US, tends to produce strong single-party governments but can be disproportionate; proportional representation, used in Norway and much of Europe, produces more representative parliaments that often require coalitions. The same votes can yield very different governments depending on the rules -- a trade-off between stability and representativeness, with no single "correct" answer. Beyond voting, citizens take part by joining parties, contacting representatives, protesting, signing petitions, boycotting and more. Voter turnout offers one health check, varying widely between countries and shaped by age, education and whether voting is compulsory. A democracy stays alive not just on election day but through continuous engagement.
